Ran `crimes context src/billing.ts` — 7 findings anchored on the file (1 high, 4 medium, 2 low), plus two `contract_drift` findings anchored on `src/api/state.ts` that name `billing.ts` as the counterparty. Risk profile is uniform: churn low, 0 importers, test gap bottom-quartile — so ranking comes down to severity × how badly the code misleads an editor.

## 1. Split `generateInvoice` into pure helpers, and make the retry loop report failure

`crime_00007` (God Function, sev 0.90 / conf 0.95, lines 50–253, 3.4× the 60-line threshold) — the highest-scoring finding on the file. Reading it confirms the detector: nine distinct responsibilities with no seams — plan pricing (69–89), loyalty discount (92–102), promo resolution (106–126), fraud scoring (129–143), country tax (146–156), currency (160–165), PII audit log (183–199), metrics (202–211), email composition (214–233), send-retry (237–250).

Extract each region as a pure function taking explicit inputs (`priceLines`, `loyaltyDiscount`, `promoDiscount`, `riskScore`, `taxCents`, `currencyFor`, `renderInvoiceEmail`) and leave `generateInvoice` as a thin orchestrator. Three other findings collapse into this one change:

- `crime_00015` (Temporal Recklessness, 7 clock reads at 57, 63, 92, 198, 238, 250) — once discount and metadata are helpers, `now` becomes a parameter and the discount tiers are testable at a pinned instant. `Math.random()` at line 56 has the same problem and isn't covered by that detector; inject an id generator alongside the clock.
- `crime_00039` (Catch and Release, 245–247) — the `catch {}` has no binding at all, so `attempts` reaches 3 and the function still returns a successful `Invoice`. Have the send helper return a typed result and record the failure in `metadata`/telemetry. This is the only finding on the file where the current behaviour is silently wrong rather than merely hard to edit.
- The tax table at 146–154 is byte-identical to `tax()` at 257–267. The scan didn't raise a duplication finding for it (both copies live in the same file), but the comment at 255 admits it: extracting the region should call `tax()` rather than re-deriving the ladder.

`crime_00037` (God File, 311 lines, 1.0× threshold) is a symptom, not a target — do the extraction first and only split the module if it's still oversized.

## 2. Fix `calculateRefundPreview` — name, side effects, and the rule that only exists in a comment

Two findings sit on the same six lines and reinforce each other:

- `crime_00017` (False Identity, conf 0.80): the `calculate…Preview` prefix promises a pure read, but lines 41–42 write an audit record and send a customer email before returning `invoice.totalCents`.
- `crime_00022` (Logic in the Alibi, conf 0.71): the comment at line 39 says *"Only owners can refund enterprise plans unless billing support approves"* — and the detector's evidence is the point: the domain terms `owner`, `plan`, `billing` appear nowhere in the body. There is no authorization check at all.

That combination is the worst agent trap in the file. An agent asked to "show a refund preview on the invoice page" will read the name, assume it's safe to call on render, and ship code that emails customers on every page load — while the authorization rule stays prose. Split it into `refundAmountCents(invoice)` (pure) and `requestRefund(user, invoice)` (side-effecting, with the owner/enterprise/support-approval rule as an executable guard that throws). Do this before #1 if you only have time for one thing that changes runtime behaviour.

## 3. Unify the `Invoice` / `User` declarations with `src/api/state.ts`

`crime_00006` carries severity 0.96 — the highest in the whole scan — and `crime_00005` 0.90, both at confidence 0.82. They don't appear in `crimes context src/billing.ts` because the finding anchors on `src/api/state.ts`, but `billing.ts` owns declaration B and is listed in `related_files`.

`Invoice` here has 11 fields; the one in `state.ts:9` has 2. The six disagreements are exactly the fields you can't afford to be wrong about: `subtotalCents`, `discountCents`, `taxCents`, `currency` (money), `userId` (identifier), `createdAt` (timestamp). Nothing in the build compares the two, so an agent adding a field to whichever declaration it loaded first gets a clean typecheck and a runtime shape that only half the codebase agrees on.

Make `state.ts` derive from the billing declaration — `type Invoice = Pick<BillingInvoice, "id" | "totalCents">` or similar — so the projection is explicit and a future field change reaches both. Same for `User` (`createdAt` present here, absent there), which `generateInvoice` reads at line 92 to compute the loyalty discount.

**Ordering caveat:** the scan's own in-file rank puts Temporal Recklessness second, ahead of the naming and comment findings. I've demoted it because injecting the clock is a natural by-product of #1 and carries no standalone behavioural risk, whereas #2 and #3 describe code that is actively misleading about what it does. Everything else on the file (`crime_00042`, 4 TODO markers) is cleanup that should ride along with whichever region you touch.
